title: Grade 11 Chemistry — Chemical Thermodynamics
description: Chapter 6: enthalpy, entropy, Gibbs free energy, laws of thermodynamics
subject: chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following is a state function?
options: Work (W)
Heat (q)
Enthalpy (H)
Both work and heat
questions.explanation: State functions depend only on the state of the system (like T, P, V), not on the path taken. Enthalpy H, internal energy U, entropy S, and Gibbs free energy G are state functions. Heat and work are path functions.

questions.question: The standard enthalpy of formation (ΔfH°) of any element in its standard state is:
options: Positive — elements release energy on formation
Negative — elements form spontaneously
Zero — by definition
Equal to its atomisation enthalpy
questions.explanation: By convention, the standard enthalpy of formation of every element in its most stable standard state is defined as zero. This provides a reference baseline for calculating reaction enthalpies.

questions.question: Hess's Law states that:
options: The enthalpy of a reaction depends on how quickly it occurs
The total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether it occurs in one step or several steps (path independence of ΔH)
Entropy always increases in any chemical process
Exothermic reactions are always spontaneous
questions.explanation: Hess's Law follows from enthalpy being a state function. This allows us to calculate ΔH for reactions that cannot be measured directly by combining known reactions.

questions.question: A reaction is exothermic when:
options: ΔH > 0 (system absorbs heat)
ΔH < 0 (system releases heat to surroundings)
ΔH = 0 (no heat change)
ΔS > 0 only
questions.explanation: Exothermic reactions release heat: ΔH < 0 (products have lower enthalpy than reactants). Examples: combustion, respiration, neutralisation. The surroundings become warmer.

questions.question: The Gibbs free energy equation is:
options: G = H + TS
ΔG = ΔH - TΔS
ΔG = ΔH + ΔS
G = H/TS
questions.explanation: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS (Gibbs-Helmholtz equation). It combines enthalpy and entropy to predict spontaneity at constant T and P. ΔG < 0 → spontaneous; ΔG > 0 → non-spontaneous; ΔG = 0 → equilibrium.

questions.question: Entropy is a measure of:
options: The heat content of a system
The degree of disorder or randomness in a system
The temperature of a system
The pressure exerted by a system
questions.explanation: Entropy (S) quantifies disorder. Gases have higher entropy than liquids, which have higher entropy than solids. A reaction producing more gas molecules increases entropy.

questions.question: The Second Law of Thermodynamics states that:
options: Energy is conserved in all processes
The entropy of the universe always increases in a spontaneous process (ΔS_universe > 0)
Heat can flow from cold to hot without work input
All reactions reach equilibrium at 0 K
questions.explanation: The Second Law: ΔS_universe = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings > 0 for any spontaneous process. The universe always moves toward greater disorder. This is why time has a direction.

questions.question: For a spontaneous reaction at constant temperature and pressure, the Gibbs free energy change (ΔG) must be:
options: Positive
Negative
Zero
Equal to the entropy change
questions.explanation: ΔG < 0 is the criterion for spontaneity at constant T and P. Spontaneous processes always move toward lower Gibbs free energy, just as objects roll toward lower potential energy.

questions.question: An endothermic reaction (ΔH > 0) can be spontaneous when:
options: At all temperatures — endothermic reactions are always spontaneous
Never — endothermic reactions cannot be spontaneous
At high temperatures where TΔS > ΔH (large positive entropy change)
When ΔG is positive
questions.explanation: From ΔG = ΔH - TΔS: if ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, then at high enough T, TΔS > ΔH, making ΔG < 0 (spontaneous). Melting ice is an example: endothermic, but spontaneous above 0°C.

questions.question: The First Law of Thermodynamics states that:
options: Energy can be created from nuclear reactions
The change in internal energy (ΔU) of a system equals heat absorbed (q) plus work done on the system (w): ΔU = q + w
Entropy is conserved in all processes
Pressure is constant during all chemical reactions
questions.explanation: The First Law is the Law of Conservation of Energy: ΔU = q + w. The internal energy of a system changes by the heat added to it minus the work done by it (or plus work done on it).

questions.question: The relationship between enthalpy change (ΔH) and internal energy change (ΔU) at constant pressure is:
options: ΔH = ΔU
ΔH = ΔU + PΔV
ΔH = ΔU × PΔV
ΔH = ΔU - PΔV
questions.explanation: H = U + PV, so ΔH = ΔU + Δ(PV) = ΔU + PΔV at constant P. For reactions involving gases: PΔV = Δng × RT, where Δng = moles of gaseous products - moles of gaseous reactants.

questions.question: For the reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), what is the sign of ΔS?
options: ΔS > 0 because products are more complex molecules
ΔS < 0 because 4 moles of gas (reactants) produce only 2 moles of gas (products), reducing disorder
ΔS = 0 because no change of state occurs
ΔS > 0 because the reaction is exothermic
questions.explanation: Going from 4 moles of gas to 2 moles of gas decreases the number of molecules (disorder), so ΔS < 0. This is one reason why the Haber process must be run at high temperature — to overcome the entropy penalty.

questions.question: The Third Law of Thermodynamics states that:
options: All reactions go to completion at 0 K
The entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero (0 K) is zero — providing a reference for absolute entropy values
Energy cannot be created at 0 K
Gibbs free energy equals zero at absolute zero
questions.explanation: The Third Law gives a universal reference point: S = 0 for a perfect crystal at 0 K. This allows calculation of absolute (standard) entropies at any temperature by integrating heat capacity from 0 K.

questions.question: The enthalpy of neutralisation of a strong acid with a strong base in dilute solution is always approximately:
options: +57.1 kJ/mol (endothermic)
-57.1 kJ/mol (exothermic)
0 kJ/mol (no change)
Depends strongly on which acid and base are used
questions.explanation: For strong acid + strong base, the net reaction is always H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), ΔH ≈ -57.1 kJ/mol. This constant value confirms that strong acids and bases are fully dissociated in dilute solution.

questions.question: Bond dissociation enthalpy is always:
options: Negative — energy is released when bonds break
Positive — energy input is always required to break bonds
Zero for all covalent bonds
Variable — some bonds release energy when broken
questions.explanation: Breaking a chemical bond always requires energy input (endothermic). Bond formation always releases energy (exothermic). The sign is always positive for bond dissociation because we are breaking bonds.

questions.question: If ΔG° = 0 for a reaction, what can be concluded?
options: The reaction is non-spontaneous in both directions
The system is at equilibrium with K = 1
The reaction is highly spontaneous
ΔH and ΔS are both zero
questions.explanation: ΔG° = -RT ln K. If ΔG° = 0, then ln K = 0, so K = 1 — reactants and products are present in equal amounts at equilibrium. The reaction proceeds spontaneously in neither direction preferentially.

questions.question: The Born-Haber cycle is used to calculate:
options: Activation energy of chemical reactions
Lattice enthalpy of ionic compounds (which cannot be measured directly)
Standard electrode potentials
Bond dissociation energies of covalent molecules
questions.explanation: The Born-Haber cycle applies Hess's Law to ionic compound formation, calculating the lattice enthalpy indirectly from measurable quantities like ionisation enthalpy, electron affinity, and sublimation enthalpy.

questions.question: Under which conditions is a reaction spontaneous regardless of temperature?
options: ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0
ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0
ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0 (exothermic AND increases entropy)
ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0
questions.explanation: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS. If ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0, then ΔG is negative at ALL temperatures — the reaction is always spontaneous. If ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0, ΔG is always positive — never spontaneous.

questions.question: The enthalpy of combustion is always:
options: Positive (endothermic)
Negative (exothermic — heat is always released during combustion)
Zero for hydrocarbons
Depends on whether the product is CO₂ or CO
questions.explanation: Combustion is always exothermic (ΔH < 0) — it releases heat. Standard enthalpy of combustion values are always negative, making combustion reactions useful for energy production.

questions.question: Kirchhoff's equation relates enthalpy change to:
options: The entropy change at different pressures
The variation of ΔH with temperature using heat capacities: ΔH₂ = ΔH₁ + ΔCp(T₂-T₁)
The Gibbs energy and activation energy of a reaction
The equilibrium constant at different temperatures
questions.explanation: Kirchhoff's equation: d(ΔH)/dT = ΔCp. Integrating: ΔH(T₂) = ΔH(T₁) + ΔCp(T₂-T₁). It allows calculation of ΔH at any temperature from a known value and heat capacity data.
